topics.title: Geographical Location, Latitudinal Extent & Extreme Points

points.html: India lies entirely in the Northern and Eastern Hemispheres, extending latitudinally from 8°4' N to 37°6' N and longitudinally from 68°7' E to 97°25' E.
The mainland of India spans 3,214 km from North to South (Indira Col in Ladakh to Cape Comorin in Kanyakumari) and 2,933 km from West to East (Guhar Moti in Gujarat to Kibithu in Arunachal Pradesh).
India covers an area of 32,87,263 sq. km (ISFR: 32,87,469 sq. km), accounting for approximately 2.4% of the world's total land area while sustaining 17.5% of the world's population (Census 2011).
India is the seventh-largest country in the world by land area, after Russia, Canada, USA, China, Brazil, and Australia.

Indira Point [इंदिरा पॉइंट] (formerly Pygmalion Point or Parsons Point) at 6°45' N latitude on Great Nicobar Island is India's southernmost geographical point; it was partially submerged during the 2004 tsunami.
Indira Col in Ladakh marks India's northernmost point; Kibithu in Anjaw district of Arunachal Pradesh marks the easternmost point; and Guhar Moti (Kutch, Gujarat) marks the westernmost point.

topics.title: International Land Frontiers, Boundaries & Coastal Borderlands

points.html: India shares 15,106.7 km of international land borders with 7 countries: Bangladesh (4,096.7 km - longest), China (3,488 km), Pakistan (3,323 km), Nepal (1,751 km), Myanmar (1,643 km), Bhutan (699 km), and Afghanistan (106 km in PoK - shortest).

The international boundary between India and Pakistan is known as the Radcliffe Line [रेडक्लिफ रेखा], drawn in August 1947 by Sir Cyril Radcliffe; Radcliffe line also demarcates the border with Bangladesh.
The McMahon Line [मैकमोहन रेखा] was drawn in 1914 at the Simla Convention to demarcate the boundary between British India and Tibet (Arunachal Pradesh sector of India-China border).

The Durand Line [डूरंड रेखा] was demarcated in 1893 by Sir Mortimer Durand between British India and Afghanistan; currently it separates Pakistan and Afghanistan, with a 106 km stretch bordering India in Ladakh (PoK).

India's total coastline measures 7,516.6 km (mainland coastline: 5,422.6 km, island territories: 2,094 km), touching 9 coastal states: Gujarat (longest coastline ~1,214.7 km), Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Kerala, Odisha, Karnataka, West Bengal, and Goa.

topics.title: Northern Mountain Region: Himalayas, Glaciers & Mountain Passes

points.html: The Himalayas are young fold mountains formed during the Tertiary period by the collision of the Indian tectonic plate with the Eurasian plate, compressing sediments of the Tethys Geosyncline.

From north to south, the Himalayas are divided into four longitudinal belts: Trans-Himalaya (Tibetan Himalayas - Karakoram, Ladakh, Zaskar), Greater Himalaya / हिमाद्रि [Himadri], Lesser / Middle Himalaya / हिमाचल [Himachal], and Outer Himalaya / शिवालिक [Shiwalik].

K2 / Godwin Austen (8,611 m) in the Karakoram Range (PoK) is the highest peak in the Indian subcontinent (2nd highest globally); Kanchenjunga (8,586 m) in Sikkim is the highest peak situated in undisputed Indian territory.

Crucial पर्वतीय दर्रे [Mountain Passes] tested by UPPSC: Zoji La (Ladakh - connects Srinagar to Leh), Banihal (J&K - Jawahar Tunnel), Shipki La (HP - Satluj enters India), Rohtang (HP - Atal Tunnel), Lipulekh, Mana and Niti (Uttarakhand - Kailash-Mansarovar route), Nathu La and Jelep La (Sikkim - Indo-China trade), and Bomdi La (Arunachal Pradesh).

Siachen Glacier [सियाचिन हिमनद] (76 km long) in the Nubra Valley of Karakoram is the world's longest glacier outside polar regions and the highest battlefield on Earth; other key हिमनद [Glaciers] include Baltoro, Biafo, Hispar, and Gangotri.
Karewa formations [करेवा] in the Kashmir Valley are thick lacustrine silt deposits of the Pleistocene period, world-renowned for the cultivation of GI-tagged Zafran (Saffron).

topics.title: Peninsular Plateau, Mountain Ranges & Highest Peaks

points.html: प्रायद्वीपीय पठार [Peninsular Plateau] is an ancient, rigid, triangular shield composed of Pre-Cambrian crystalline and metamorphic rocks, constituting the oldest geological landmass of India (part of Gondwanaland).

Aravalli Range [अरावली श्रेणी] is the oldest fold mountain system in India and one of the oldest in the world (Pre-Cambrian era, now residual mountains); its highest peak is Guru Shikhar (1,722 m) at Mount Abu in Rajasthan.

Western Ghats / सह्याद्रि [Sahyadri] form a continuous escarpment from Tapti valley to Kanyakumari; pierced by four major दर्रे [Mountain Passes]: Thal Ghat (Mumbai-Nashik), Bhor Ghat (Mumbai-Pune), Pal Ghat (Palakkad Gap - Kochi-Coimbatore), and Shencottah Gap.
Western Ghats and Eastern Ghats converge at the Nilgiri Hills [नीलगिरि पहाड़ियाँ] ('Blue Mountains'); Doddabetta (2,637 m) is the highest peak of the Nilgiris.
Anamudi [अनाईमुडी] (2,695 m) in the Anaimalai Hills of Kerala is the highest mountain peak in South India and the entire Peninsular region.
Vindhya and Satpura ranges run parallel across central India; Dhupgarh (1,350 m) near Pachmarhi on Mahadeo Hills is the highest peak of the Satpura Range.

Shillong Plateau / Meghalaya Plateau is a detached eastern extension of the प्रायद्वीपीय पठार [Peninsular Plateau] (not part of the Himalayas), separated from the Rajmahal Hills by the Malda Gap (Garo-Rajmahal Gap).

topics.title: Great Northern Plains, Coastal Belts & Island Groups

points.html: The Great Plains of North India are formed by the deep aggradational deposition of alluvium brought by the Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra river systems into a massive foredeep depression.

The plains feature three distinct longitudinal belts: भाबर [Bhabhar] (8-16 km wide pebble/gravel belt along the Shiwalik foot where streams disappear), तराई [Terai] (marshy, humid, densely forested belt south of Bhabhar where streams re-emerge), and the vast जलोढ़ मैदान [Alluvial Plain].
The जलोढ़ [Alluvial] plains comprise older elevated alluvium containing calcareous kankar nodules called बांगर [Bangar], and younger, highly fertile floodplains renewed annually called खादर [Khadar].

Jarawa, Sentinelese, Onge, and Great Andamanese are indigenous hunter-gatherer tribes of Negrito stock inhabiting the Andaman Islands, classified as Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs).
Garo, Khasi, and Jaintia tribes of Meghalaya follow a traditional matrilineal descent and matrilocal residence system.

Lepcha and Bhutia tribes inhabit Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills of West Bengal; Bodo and Miri tribes are indigenous to Assam; Chenchu tribe inhabits the Nallamala forests of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.

title: Languages of India
gist: Indian languages belong to four major families: Indo-Aryan (~78%), Dravidian (~20%), Austro-Asiatic (Munda), and Sino-Tibetan. The Eighth Schedule recognizes 22 official languages, with Hindi and Bengali being the most widely spoken, while UP recognizes Hindi and Urdu.

topics.title: Linguistic Families of India & Major Language Groups

points.html: The Indo-Aryan language family [भारतीय-आर्य भाषा परिवार] is the largest linguistic group in India, spoken by approximately 78% of the population, comprising Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi, Sindhi, Odia, Assamese, and Sanskrit.

The Dravidian language family [द्रविड़ भाषा परिवार] is the second largest group (~20% speakers), comprising the major literary languages Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, and Malayalam, along with tribal languages like Gondi, Kurukh, and Kui.

The Austro-Asiatic (Munda) family [ऑस्ट्रो-एशियाटिक भाषा परिवार] is spoken primarily by indigenous tribes of central and eastern India, including Santhali, Mundari, Ho, Bhumij, and Khasi in Meghalaya.
Hindi is the most widely spoken language in India (~43.6% native speakers as per Census 2011), followed by Bengali (8.03%), Marathi (6.86%), Telugu (6.7%), and Tamil (5.7%).
According to Ethnologue 2025, Bengali ranks as the 7th most spoken language in the world (~284 million global users) and the second most spoken in the Indian subcontinent after Hindi.

topics.title: Scheduled Languages, Classical Status & UP Official Languages

points.html: The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution originally listed 14 regional languages in 1950, which has expanded to 22 recognized scheduled languages through three constitutional amendments.

Sindhi was added to the Eighth Schedule by the 21st Constitutional Amendment Act (1967); Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali were added by the 71st Amendment (1992); Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali were added by the 92nd Amendment (2003).

The Government of India confers Classical Language status [शास्त्रीय भाषा] based on high antiquity of early texts (1500-2000 years); Tamil was declared first in 2004, followed by Sanskrit (2005), Telugu and Kannada (2008), Malayalam (2013), and Odia (2014).
In October 2024, five additional languages were granted Classical status: Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese, and Bengali, bringing the total to 11 Classical Languages.

Uttar Pradesh has two officially recognized state languages: Hindi was declared the first official language in 1947, and Urdu was enacted as the second official language through the UP Official Language (Amendment) Act 1989.

topics.title: Himalayan Drainage System: Ganga, Indus & Brahmaputra Basins

points.html: The Himalayan अपवाह तंत्र [Drainage System] comprises perennial antecedent rivers originating in trans-Himalayan हिमनद [Glaciers]: the Indus, the Ganga, and the Brahmaputra, cutting dramatic deep gorges across the mountain wall.

Ganga River (2,525 km - India's longest river) originates as the Bhagirathi from Gangotri हिमनद [Glacier] at Gaumukh (Uttarkashi); at Devprayag [देवप्रयाग], Bhagirathi merges with Alaknanda to form the Ganga.

Panch Prayag [पंच प्रयाग] along the Alaknanda in downstream order: Vishnuprayag (Alaknanda + Dhauliganga), Nandprayag (Alaknanda + Nandakini), Karnaprayag (Alaknanda + Pindar), Rudraprayag (Alaknanda + Mandakini), and Devprayag (Alaknanda + Bhagirathi).
Major left-bank tributaries of Ganga include Ramganga, Gomti, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi (known as 'Sorrow of Bihar' for catastrophic course shifts), and Mahananda.

Indus River (Sindhu, 2,880 km total, 1,114 km in India) rises near Mansarovar Lake in Tibet; key tributaries form the Panjnad: Jhelum (originates Verinag, flows through Wular Lake), Chenab (Chandra-Bhaga confluence, largest tributary), Ravi, Beas, and Satluj (rises at Rakshastal near Mansarovar).

Brahmaputra rises from Chemayungdung/Angsi हिमनद [Glacier] in Tibet as the Yarlung Tsangpo; cuts around Namcha Barwa entering Arunachal Pradesh as Siang/Dihang; forms Majuli (world's largest river island) in Assam; enters Bangladesh as the Jamuna and merges with the Padma (Ganga).

topics.title: Mechanism of Indian Monsoon & Rainfall Distribution

points.html: India's climate is classified as Tropical Monsoon [उष्णकटिबंधीय मानसूनी जलवायु], characterized by seasonal reversal of wind direction driven by differential heating of land and sea and shift of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ).

दक्षिण-पश्चिम मानसून [South-West Monsoon] (June to September) advances across India in two main branches: the Arabian Sea Branch and the Bay of Bengal Branch, supplying over 75% of India's total annual precipitation.
Mawsynram and Cherrapunji on the southern slopes of Khasi Hills in Meghalaya receive the highest average annual rainfall in the world (>1,100 cm) due to the funneling relief of the Meghalaya plateau.

The windward western slopes of the Western Ghats receive heavy orographic rainfall exceeding 250 cm, while the leeward Deccan plateau lies in the rain-shadow zone [वृष्टि छाया क्षेत्र] receiving under 60 cm.

Global climatic oscillations significantly influence monsoon performance: El Niño generally suppresses Indian monsoon rainfall, whereas La Niña and positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) phases promote abundant monsoon rains.

topics.title: Western Disturbances, Winter Rainfall & UP Climate Dynamics

points.html: पश्चिमी विक्षोभ [Western Disturbances] are extra-tropical temperate cyclonic storms originating over the Mediterranean Sea, steered into northwest India by the subtropical westerly jet stream during winter months (December–February).

पश्चिमी विक्षोभ [Western Disturbances] bring light to moderate winter rainfall to Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, and Western Uttar Pradesh, which is immensely beneficial for the रबी [Rabi] wheat crop, while causing heavy snowfall in the Western Himalayas.

topics.title: Major Soil Groups of India: Alluvial, Black, Red & Laterite

points.html: The Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) classifies Indian soils into 8 major categories, among which जलोढ़ मिट्टी [Alluvial Soil], काली मिट्टी [Black Soil], लाल मिट्टी [Red Soil], and लैटेराइट मिट्टी [Laterite Soil] are commercially paramount.

जलोढ़ मिट्टी [Alluvial Soil] is India's most widespread and productive soil group (~40% area), formed by river deposition in the Indo-Gangetic-Brahmaputra plains and coastal deltas; rich in potash and lime, but deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus, and organic humus.

काली मिट्टी [Black Soil / रेगुर [Regur]] (काली मिट्टी [Black Cotton Soil]) is derived from the weathering of Deccan basaltic lava (Maharashtra, Gujarat, western MP); dominated by montmorillonite clay, high moisture retention, swells when wet, and develops deep cracks when dry, conferring a 'self-ploughing' [स्वतः जुताई] attribute ideal for dryland cotton cultivation.

लाल मिट्टी [Red Soil] develops on crystalline igneous Archean rocks under low rainfall; its red hue is caused by wide diffusion of iron oxides (ferric oxide); highly porous, poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, and humus, requiring irrigation for crops.

लैटेराइट मिट्टी [Laterite Soil] forms under high temperatures and alternating intense wet and dry spells through severe leaching [निक्षालन]; rich in iron oxide and aluminium residues, but acidic and poor in lime, silica, and potash; ideal for रोपण फसलें [Plantation Crops] (tea, coffee, rubber, cashew).

points.html: In Uttar Pradesh, the northern sub-Himalayan belt is divided into: भाबर [Bhabhar] (a narrow gravelly boulder tract where rivers sink underground) and तराई [Terai] (a damp, swampy, silt-rich जलोढ़ [Alluvial] zone south of Bhabhar, highly fertile for sugarcane and paddy).

The Gangetic plain of UP comprises two broad जलोढ़ [Alluvial] types: खादर [Khadar] (newer, light-colored floodplains renewed annually by flood silts, highly fertile) and बांगर [Bangar] (older upland alluvium characterized by calcareous nodules called कंकड़ [Kankar], less fertile).

Bundelkhand plateau soils [बुंदेलखंड की मिट्टियाँ] in southern UP are locally divided into: Rakar [राकर] (red gravelly soil on slopes), Parwa [पड़वा] (yellow-grey sandy loam), Mar [मार] (fertile black clay soil), and Kabar [काबर] (sticky dark काली मिट्टी [Black Soil]).

Saline and Alkaline soils (locally designated as ऊसर [Usar], रेह [Reh], or कल्लर [Kallar]) are widespread in semi-arid canal-irrigated districts of central UP (Mainpuri, Aligarh, Etah, Kanpur, Raebareli, Unnao); reclaimed by application of gypsum and pyrite.
Severe soil erosion occurs in the Chambal and Yamuna basins (Agra, Etawah, Jalaun districts) due to intense gully erosion [अवनलिका अपरदन], forming deep badland ravines [बीहड़].

points.html: Tube-wells and open wells constitute the largest source of irrigation in India (~62%), followed by government and private Canals (~24%), Tanks (~3%), and other sources.
Uttar Pradesh ranks #1 in India in net irrigated area and #1 in tubewell-irrigated area, with tube-wells irrigating approximately 80% of the state's net cultivated land.

Tanks [तालाब] are the dominant traditional irrigation source in Peninsular South India (Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana) due to the undulating crystalline rocky terrain, which prevents canal excavation and promotes rainwater harvesting in natural depressions.

Canal irrigation is most extensively developed in the northern जलोढ़ [Alluvial] plains of Punjab, Haryana, and Uttar Pradesh due to perennial snow-fed rivers and soft, easily excavated alluvial soils.
Micro-irrigation techniques (Drip and Sprinkler irrigation under Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana - PMKSY) are heavily promoted for water-use efficiency in water-stressed arid regions.

The Tarai region of UP receives high rainfall and has rich alluvium, favoring sugarcane and paddy; the Bundelkhand and Vindhyan zones suffer from moisture stress, specializing in दलहन [Pulses], तिलहन [Oilseeds], and millets.

topics.title: Cropping Seasons (Kharif, Rabi, Zaid) & Operational Landholdings

points.html: India features three distinct cropping seasons: खरीफ [Kharif] (June–July to Sept–Oct, monsoon crops: Rice, Maize, Jowar, Bajra, Cotton, Jute, Arhar), रबी [Rabi] (October–December to March–April, winter crops: Wheat, Barley, Gram, Mustard, Peas), and जायद [Zaid] (short summer season March–June: Watermelon, Muskmelon, Cucumber, Vegetables).
Operational landholdings in India are categorized into 5 classes: Marginal (<1 hectare), Small (1–2 hectares), Semi-Medium (2–4 hectares), Medium (4–10 hectares), and Large (>10 hectares).
According to Agricultural Census data, Marginal and Small farmers constitute approximately 86% of all operational agricultural holdings in India, reflecting acute land fragmentation.
Net Sown Area constitutes roughly 43-45% of India's total geographical area, with the cropping intensity hovering around 140-145%.
Uttar Pradesh ranks #1 in India in total foodgrain production, contributing nearly 18-19% of national foodgrain output.

topics.title: Genesis, Inputs & High Yielding Varieties of Green Revolution

points.html: हरित क्रांति [Green Revolution] in India was launched in 1966-67 (during the Annual Plans period) to overcome severe food deficits and end reliance on US PL-480 food imports.

Dr. Norman Ernest Borlaug (USA/CIMMYT Mexico) is recognized as the 'Father of the हरित क्रांति [Green Revolution] in the World'; he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970 for breeding high-yielding semi-dwarf wheat varieties using Norin-10 dwarfing genes.

Dr. M.S. Swaminathan [डॉ. एम.एस. स्वामीनाथन] is revered as the 'Father of the हरित क्रांति [Green Revolution] in India', spearheading the adaptation and field deployment of Mexican semi-dwarf varieties (Lerma Rojo 64A and Sonora 64).

Govind Ballabh Pant University of Agriculture & Technology (Pantnagar, established in 1960 in erstwhile UP, now Uttarakhand) served as the pioneering cradle of the हरित क्रांति [Green Revolution] in India.

The technological package of the हरित क्रांति [Green Revolution] relied on the synergistic 'seed-fertilizer-water technology': High-Yielding Variety (HYV) seeds, assured tubewell/canal irrigation, chemical fertilizers (ideal NPK ratio 4:2:1), and plant protection pesticides.

topics.title: Crop-Wise Impact, Western UP Lead & Agricultural Revolutions

points.html: The हरित क्रांति [Green Revolution] disproportionately benefited Wheat [गेहूं] production (often termed a 'Wheat Revolution'), followed secondarily by Rice; coarse cereals (millets) and दलहन [Pulses] experienced stagnant or negative relative growth.

Geographically, the First हरित क्रांति [Green Revolution] was heavily concentrated in Punjab, Haryana, and Western Uttar Pradesh (Meerut, Muzaffarnagar, Bulandshahr, Aligarh) due to preexisting canal infrastructure and progressive farming.
Dr. M.S. Swaminathan later advocated for an 'Evergreen Revolution' [सदाबहार क्रांति], emphasizing productivity improvement in perpetuity without causing ecological or social harm.

Rainbow Revolution [इंद्रधनुषी क्रांति] encompasses the integrated development of all agricultural sectors: Green (foodgrains), White (milk / Operation Flood), Yellow (तिलहन [Oilseeds]), Blue (fisheries), Golden (fruits/horticulture/honey), Grey (fertilizers), Silver (eggs/poultry), and Round (potato).

points.html: Cotton [कपास] ('White Gold') is a tropical/subtropical खरीफ [Kharif] cash crop requiring 210 frost-free days, abundant sunshine, and light rainfall (50-100 cm); thrives best in the deep moisture-retentive काली मिट्टी [Black Cotton Soil / रेगुर [Regur]] of the Deccan Trap.

Jute [जूट] ('Golden Fibre' / सुनहरा रेशा) requires hot and humid climate (>27°C, >150 cm rainfall) and fertile river silt renewed annually by floods.

West Bengal is the overwhelming leader in Jute production, contributing over 75-80% of India's total raw jute, concentrated in the fertile जलोढ़ [Alluvial] floodplains of the lower Ganga (Hooghly basin).

Gram [चना] (Chickpea) is the single most important pulse crop in India, accounting for nearly 40-45% of total pulse production; a रबी [Rabi] crop cultivated on light loamy and clayey soils; prominent varieties include 'Radhey', 'Pusa-256' (KBG-38), and 'Avarodhi' (wilt-resistant).

Moong (Green gram) and Urad (Black gram) are short-duration दलहन [Pulses] cultivated in both खरीफ [Kharif] and जायद [Zaid] seasons, fitting well into crop rotations.

topics.title: Shifting Cultivation: Agronomic Practices & Ecological Effects

points.html: झूम कृषि [Shifting Cultivation] (Slash-and-Burn agriculture / कर्तन एवं दहन प्रणाली) is a primitive subsistence farming system where a patch of forest is cleared by felling and burning vegetation, cultivated for 2-3 years, and then abandoned to fallow for natural regeneration.
Ash from burnt trees adds potash to the soil temporarily, but the rapid decline in natural soil fertility and weed infestation forces tribes to shift to a fresh forest plot.

Shortening of the fallow cycle (from 15-20 years historically to 2-4 years currently) due to population pressure has caused catastrophic deforestation, accelerated soil erosion, and biodiversity loss.

झूम कृषि [Shifting Cultivation] is most prevalent among indigenous tribal communities inhabiting the hill tracts of Northeast India (Assam, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Mizoram, Manipur, and Arunachal Pradesh).

Kumari [कुमारी]: Western Ghats hill tracts in Kerala and Karnataka.
Valre [वालरे] or Waltre [वाल्टरे]: South-eastern Rajasthan (practiced by Bhils).
Khil [खिल]: Himalayan belt of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.
Kuruwa [कुरुवा]: Santhal Pargana and Chota Nagpur plateau in Jharkhand.
Penda [पेंडा]: Bastar district of Chhattisgarh.

points.html: Uttar Pradesh ranks #1 among all Indian states in total milk production and possesses the largest buffalo population in the country.

Bhadawari [भदावरी] buffalo breed, native to the Chambal/Yamuna ravines of Agra and Etawah in UP and Bhind in MP, produces milk with the highest butterfat content (up to 12-13%) among all cattle breeds.
Murrah [मुर्राह] buffalo, originating in Haryana and Punjab, is known as 'Black Gold' for its exceptionally high daily milk yield.

topics.title: Metallic Ores: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Copper, Lead & Zinc

points.html: Dharwar rock system [धारवाड़ शैल तंत्र] is the oldest metamorphosed sedimentary rock formation in India and is the richest reservoir of metallic minerals (लौह अयस्क [Iron Ore], manganese, copper, lead, gold).

लौह अयस्क [Iron Ore] [लौह अयस्क] in India is predominantly high-grade Haematite (60-70% Fe) and Magnetite (black ore); Odisha is the leading producer (Barabil-Koira valley, Badampahar, Gorumahisani in Mayurbhanj).

Bailadila mines [बैलाडीला] in Dantewada district of Chhattisgarh produce super-high-grade haematite ore, exported to Japan through Visakhapatnam port; Kudremukh in Karnataka has major magnetite deposits.
बॉक्साइट [Bauxite] [बॉक्साइट] is the primary ore of aluminium; Odisha ranks #1 in India (Panchpatmali in Koraput district), followed by Gujarat and Jharkhand (Lohardaga).

Copper [तांबा] occurs in metamorphic rocks; Malanjkhand in Balaghat district of Madhya Pradesh is India's largest open-cast copper mine; Khetri in Jhunjhunu district of Rajasthan is a historic copper belt operated by HCL.
Rampur-Agucha in Bhilwara district and Zawar mines in Udaipur (Rajasthan) are India's richest Lead and Zinc deposits, operated by Hindustan Zinc Ltd.

topics.title: Universe Origin, Big Bang & Stellar Lifecycles

points.html: The first rational perspective regarding the origin of the planets was probably proposed by a French naturalist ‘Comte de Buffon’ in 1749. According to the number of stars participating in the origin of planets, the scientific concepts have been divided into two parts- (1) Monistic concept and (2) Dualistic concept.
The latest theory regarding the origin of the universe is the महाविस्फोट सिद्धांत [Big Bang Theory] Theory.

After the explosion, the universe expanded in all directions and different galaxies of different shapes were formed. Thus, the universe comprises of an infinite number of galaxies. It is estimated that there are appx. 100-200 billion galaxies in the universe and every galaxy is estimated to have around 100 billion stars. Our galaxy is known as an Akash Ganga or मंदाकिनी [Milky Way Galaxy].
In 2005, the Spitzer Space Telescope gave clear evidences that our galaxy (the मंदाकिनी [Milky Way Galaxy]) is barred spiral in shape, hence disapproving the earlier theories.

The formation of the star passes through different phases. In the first phase, a proto-star is formed after that the star enters the second phase i.e., the main sequence Star. A star of the size of our sun stays in this phase for around 9 or 10 billion years. After this phase, the fuel of the star i.e., hydrogen starts getting used up to an extent that the star enters the third phase i.e., towards its death.
In this phase, the outer layer of the star expands greatly, It becomes a Red Giant or Red Supergiant.

topics.title: The Solar System, Sun & Planetary Dynamics

points.html: Under the Monistic concept, Immanuel Kant’s Gaseous Hypothesis and Pierre-Simon Laplace’s Nebular Hypothesis became famous. Under the Dualistic concept, Chamberlin and Moulton Planetesimal Hypothesis, James Jeans and Jefferys Tidal Hypothesis, H.N. Russell and Lyttleton Binary Star Hypothesis etc. became noteworthy.

Georges Lemaitre (1894-1966) was the first to present the idea of an expanding universe. Later in 1967, Robert Wagoner presented the interpretation of this theory. The महाविस्फोट सिद्धांत [Big Bang Theory] theory explains how 13.7 or 13.8 billion years ago universe expanded from a very high density and high-temperature state.
The shape of the Galaxies varies in shape and size. Some are spiral, some are irregular and some are elliptical.

The universe is a collection of infinite galaxies. Every galaxy has around 100 billion stars. These stars are formed as a result of the presence of hydrogen and helium gases in their unified form (Nebulae). The gravitational force keeps the gases and dust particles in the unified form. Velocity, high temperature and organizational processes are the factors behind the formation of a star.

The lifespan of any star depends upon its size. A star of the size of our sun (one solar mass) has a lifespan of around 9 or 10 billion years. The bigger the star is, the shorter is its life span. For example, a star whose surface temperature is more than 30000 Kelvin and which is 100 times the size of our sun has a life span of only a few million years. After the main sequence life of the star ends, it enters in the elderly phase.

After the red Giant phase, a star witnesses an explosion in the form of a Nova or Supernova, thus entering its last stage of life. Depending upon its size it can end up in- a Black Dwarf, Neutron star or a कृष्ण विवर [Black Hole]. Sun like small stars – after the Red Giant phase and Nova explosion if the stellar mass is less than 1.44 solar Masses, the star will end up being a White Dwarf first and then into a Black Dwarf. Medium sized stars - after the Red Giant Phase and Supernova explosion, if the stellar mass is between 1.44 to 3 solar masses, then a star can convert into a Neutron Star (Pulsar). Large size stars – those which have a stellar mass more than 3 times that of our sun. These stars have the possibility to convert into a black hole after a supernova explosion.

points.html: अक्षांश [Latitude] is the angular distance of a point on the earth’s surface, measured in degrees from the center of the earth.

The latitude angle is denoted by the Greek lowercase letter Phi (). 0o latitude is also known as the equator. It is halfway between the North Pole and the South Pole. The equator thus divides the planet into the Northern and Southern hemisphere. The earth is widest at the equator. All other latitudes are smaller than the equator.
The 23.5o N latitude in the Northern Hemisphere is known as the कर्क रेखा [Tropic of Cancer] whereas the 66.5o N latitude in the Northern Hemisphere is known as Arctic Circle.

The 0o latitude (equator) and 0o longitude (प्रधान मध्याह्न रेखा [Prime Meridian]) intersect each other in the Gulf of Guinea located on the western coast of Africa. The Gulf is located in the Atlantic Ocean. The north and south of any place on a globe or a map is determined by latitudes. The latitudinal value in degrees of any place is directly proportional to its extent in the north of the equator for example - Beijing (China) - 39o55'N, New Delhi - 28 o38'N, New York (USA) - 40 o45' N and Rome (Italy) - 41 o54' N. Hence among these Rome is the most northern city.

points.html: (a) Both Statement-II and Statement-III are correct and both of them explain Statement-I (b) Both Statement-II and Statement-III are correct, but only one of them explains Statement-I (c) Only one of the Statements-II and-III is correct and that explains Statement-I (d) Neither Statement-II nor Statement-III is correct I.A.S. (Pr e) 2024 Ans. (a) Chemical weathering is the process that breaks down rock through chemical changes. Rainfall and temperature can affect the rate at which rocks weather. High temperatures and greater rainfall increase the rate of chemical weathering. Rocks in tropical regions exposed to abundant rainfall and hot temperatures weather much faster than similar rocks residing in cold, dry regions. Rainwater may contain impurities from the atmosphere in the form of dust particles and dissolved gases like oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide. When water (e.g. rainwater) mixes with carbon dioxide gas in the air or in air pockets in soil, a weak acid solution, called carbonic acid, is produced. When carbonic acid flows through the cracks of some rocks, it chemically reacts with the rock causing some of it to dissolve. This process is called carbonation. It is very active in limestone regions. Rainwater contains dissolved oxygen from the atmosphere, which can participate in oxidation processes that contribute to weathering. Oxygen in rainwater reacts with minerals, particularly iron-bearing ones, to form oxides or rust, leading to weakening and breakdown. Hence, both Statement-II and Statement-III are correct and both of them explain Statement-I. The ज्वालामुखी [Volcano]

Among the gases emitted through a volcanic eruption the, highest quantity is that of water vapor (H2O). Other gases emitted are carbon-dioxide (CO2), sulphur dioxide (SO2), hydrogen (H2), carbon-monoxide (CO), hydrogen chloride (HCl), hydrogen fluoride (HF) and helium (He). Magma is made of molten rock and is stored in the Earth’s interior. lava is magma that reaches the Earth's surface with temperature ranging from about 600oC 1200oC. When Lava reaches the surface it cools to form igneous rocks. The composition of almost all lava of the earth’s crust is dominated by silica (SiO2) materials. Based on the silicate, lava can be classified into two types- Acidic Lava and Basic Lava.
Intrusive igneous rocks are formed when lava cools and solidifies before reaching the earth’s surface. Igneous rocks are of two types – intrusive and extrusive.

A geyser is a spring characterized by intermittent discharge of water ejected turbulently and accompanied by steam. Generally, all Geyser field sites are located near the active volcanic areas, and the geyser effect is due to the proximity of magma. For example the Old Faithful Geyser of Yellowstone National Park in the United States of America.

points.html: A continent is one of several very large land masses of the world. Ordered from the largest in area to the smallest, they are – Asia (44568500km 2), Africa (30065000km 2), North America (24473000km2), South America (17819000 km2), Antarctica (14200000km2), Europe (9948000km2) and Australia (7741220 km 2). Area wise Australia is the smallest continent. According to Philip’s Atlas the total land area of the various continents in proportion to the Earth is as follows – Asia 29.8%, Africa 20.3%, North America 16.2%, South America 11.8%, Antarctica 9.2%, Europe 6.8% and Australia 5.9%.
The Red Sea and Suez नहर [Canal] separate Asia from Africa. In the east, the Bering जलडमरूमध्य [Strait] separates it from North America.

Africa is the second largest continent after Asia. The three important latitudes (कर्क रेखा [Tropic of Cancer], मकर रेखा [Tropic of Capricorn] and Equator) pass through Africa. There are 54 countries in the continent of Africa more than any other continent in the world.

North America is a continent entirely within the Northern Hemisphere and all within the Western Hemisphere. The continent has been named after the Italian explorer Amerigo Vespucci. There are 23 countries in this continent. It is bordered to the north by the Arctic Ocean, to the east by the Atlantic Ocean and to the west by the Pacific Ocean. South America, Middle America, Mexico and the West Indies are collectively known as Latin America.

Antarctica is Earth’s southernmost continent. It contains the geographic South Pole and is situated, almost entirely south of the Antarctic Circle. Antarctica, on average, is the coldest, driest and windiest, and has the highest average elevation of all the continents.
The point where the energy is released is called the focus of an earthquake. The point/place where the seismic waves are first recorded is called the epicentre. UPPSC

Norway is the best-suited example of the phenomenon of Midnight Sun even though parts of other countries like Canada, Sweden, Russia, Iceland, and Finland are also located north of the Arctic Circle and experience a Midnight Sun.

points.html: लवणता [Salinity] is the amount of salt dissolved in a body of water. On average, seawater in the world’s oceans has a salinity of approximately 35‰ or 35 parts per thousand. This means that for every 1 kg (1000 grams) of seawater there are 35g of salt dissolved in it.

During an exploration of Challenger Deep in 1884, Dittmar discooured that there are 47 types of salts present in the seas. Out of these 47 types of salts, 7 are the important ones. They are as follows. Salt लवणता [Salinity] (‰) Percentage (%) of total dissolved salt Sodium Chloride 27.213 77.8 Magnesium Chloride 3.807 10.9 Magnesium Sulphate 1.658 4.7 Calcium Sulphate 1.260 3.6 Potassium Sulphate 0.863 2.5 Calcium Carbonate 0.123 0.3 Magnesium Bromide 0.076 0.2

The salinity of the ocean can be divided into horizontal and vertical parameters. The uncertainty regarding the amount of salinity in the vertical dimension has obstructed the devlopment of a principle for measuring vertical salinity. This is because in some places, salinity increases with depth and vice-versa.

The horizontal distribution of salinity in ocean water is expressed as the degree of saltiness of the water, either as a percentage or more often in parts per thousand Variations are shown in salinity distribution maps by isohalines (lines joining places having an equal degree of salinity). अक्षांश [Latitudes] have a huge impact on the salinity of the oceans. लवणता [Salinity] is lower than the average 34‰ in equatorial waters because of the heavy daily rainfall and high evaporation. मरुस्थल [Deserts] mainly 25º–30º N and S, waters have high salinity because of the high rate of evaporation caused by high temperatures and low humidity. Waters of the polar region have a salinity of less than 35‰ due to the colder climate with little evaporation and because much fresh water is added from the melting of icebergs as well as by several large poleward-bound rivers, e.g. Ob, Lena, Yenisei etc.

Ocean water of the Indian Ocean falling between 0º-10º अक्षांश [Latitudes] has a salinity of 35.14‰ however it decreases to 30‰ in Bay of Bengal. On the contrary the salinity increases upto 36‰ in the Arabian Sea. This is due to a high rate of evaporation and low humidity. Additionally there is much less fresh water carried to the Arabian Sea by west flowing rivers as compared to Bay of Bengal.

When the Sun, the Moon and the Earth are aligned in a straight line, we experience a दीर्घ ज्वार [Spring Tide]. In astronomy, this situation is known as syzygy. On the other hand, when the Sun, the Moon and the Earth are at a right angle to each other the gravitational forces of these celestial bodies act against each other resulting in लघु ज्वार [Neap Tide]. Neap Tide is observed on the 7th or 8th day of each lunar month (14 days appx.) During Neap ज्वार-भाटा [Tides], there is a decrease of 20% in the Spring Tides whereas the Neap Tides are higher than the normal occurrences.
The effect of Moon on the tidal forces of our planet is 2.17 times greater than that of the Sun.

ज्वार-भाटा [Tides] are the rise and fall of sea levels caused by the combined effects of the gravitational forces exerted by the Moon and the Sun, and the rotation of the Earth. The rotation of the Earth creates two forces - the centripetal and centrifugal forces, which play a major role in the formation of tides. This means that the side of the Earth that faces the Moon experiences a gravitational force, greater than that of the Earth itself. Hence we experience high tides. On the other hand the side of Earth that is facing away from moon experiences less gravitational force from the Moon, as a result, we experience high (indirect high tides) tides. Between these two high tides water level goes down this is called low tides (ebb). Thus in the time span of 24 hrs. and 50 minutes (or 52 minutes) we experience two High Tides and two Low Tides. Moon Syzygy Sun Moon Moon Sun Moon
The Moon is the closest celestial body to Earth hence its gravity has a significant impact on our planet. The moon is responsible for the sea waves of the oceans.
The city of Southampton in England experiences 4 tides every day. This occurs because two tides travel from English Channel and two from the North Sea at different intervals.
The gravitational tide-generating force of the Moon is approximately 2.17 times greater than that of the Sun due to its proximity. UPPSC
Spring tides occur during syzygy (New Moon and Full Moon) when Sun, Moon, and Earth align in a straight line, producing maximum tidal range. UPPSC

points.html: The atmosphere is composed of various gases, of which 99% is made up of nitrogen and oxygen. Other 1% comprises argon, carbon dioxide, neon, krypton, helium, Hydrogen, and xenon. Gas Formula Presence in वायुमंडल [Atmosphere] (in percentage) Nitrogen N 2 78.084 Oxygen O 2 20.947 Argon Ar 0.934 Carbon dioxide CO2 0.0426 Neon Ne 0.0018 Helium He 0.0005 Krypton Kr 0.0001 Hydrogen H 2 0.000053 Xenon Xe 0.000009 ∗Heavy gases in the atmosphere descend whereas lighter gases are found in the upper layers as they ascend. As a result CO2 gases extend up to 20 km from the surface, oxygen, and nitrogen up to 100 km, hydrogen up to 125 km and other gases rise far above 125 km except ozone. The atmosphere is made up of different layers of gases with varying densities and temperatures. Based on these factors different layers of the atmosphere are as follows- (1) क्षोभमंडल [Troposphere] – The lowest layer of the atmosphere is called troposphere. All weather activities like clouds, hail, fog, blizzards, thunder, windstorms, etc. are confined to the troposphere. The most important characteristic of the troposphere is that there is a decrease of 6.5 o C with an increase of every 1000 m in altitude. This decrease in temperature with an increase in altitude is known as normal lapse rate. The upper boundary of the troposphere is called tropopause. (2) समतापमंडल [Stratosphere] – Stratosphere (15-50 km) is the second most important layer of the atmosphere. It lies between mesosphere (above) and troposphere (below). This layer of atmosphere is very dry in nature and has the least amount of water vapor in it. As a result, there is no weather activity in stratosphere. The stratosphere is used for aviation purposes as the absence of weather activities makes this layer ideal for flying. Ozone layer is found in this sphere. (3) मध्यमंडल [Mesosphere] – This layer is found at an altitude of 50 to 80 km. The upper ceiling of mesosphere is called mesopause. (4) आयनमंडल [Ionosphere] – It is an electrically conducting layer, that makes radio wave transmission possible over long distances. Ionosphere extends from 80 to 640 km.

An isobar is an imaginary line that connects points having same atmospheric pressure at mean sea level. ∗Based on the process of origin, pressure belts can be divided into two parts- (1) Based on thermogenesis – pressure belts thus formed are equatorial low-pressure belts and polar high-pressure belts. (2) Based on motion-pressure belts thus formed are sub- tropical high-pressure belts and sub-polar low-pressure belts. ∗Equatorial Low-Pressure Belts – The belt extends between 5o north and south of Equator. The equator receives vertical rays of the sun throughout the year. As a result, the air gets heated and starts rising up. Hence the region always experiences low pressure. The surface air of the region moves with very slow velocity as a result of which the environment here is quite calm. This is the reason this pressure belt is also called शांत कटिबंध / डोलड्रम्स [Doldrums]. • Sub-tropical High-Pressure Belt – the belt is found between 30o-35o latitudes in both hemispheres. The air rising from the equator starts becoming cooler in the upper layers of atmosphere and hence begins sinking near 30o-35o latitudes. Simultaneously the air from the sub-polar low-pressure belts also starts descending in this region due to Earth's rotation thus a high-pressure zone is created which gives birth to sub- tropical high pressure belt. The pressure belt is highly mobile in nature, thus it is also called Horse अक्षांश [Latitude]. • Sub-Polar Low-Pressure Belt – This pressure belt is found between 60o-65o latitudes in both hemispheres. Though the temperature in this region is low throughout the year the region experiences low pressure. This is due to the fact that rotation of the Earth causes the air to spread and displaces it. As a result low pressure is created. • Polar High-Pressure Belts – The poles and the regions in close proximity to them experience high pressure because the region is very cold which causes the air to become heavy and start descending creating high pressure.

points.html: The movement of air as a result of the difference in horizontal air pressure is known as wind. Wind in general flows from a high- pressure area to a low-pressure area. If the earth were still and flat, the winds would blow from a high-pressure area directly to a low-pressure area along the isobaric lines at an angle of 90o. However, the Earth is geoid in shape and rotates on its own axis. Hence winds under the influence of dynamic forces keep shifting their trajectory. Types of Winds – There are basically three types of wind- Planetary Winds – Winds blowing constantly in a particular direction throughout the year are called planetary winds. The main planetary winds are – trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies.

पछुआ पवनें [Westerlies]- They blow from sub-tropical high-pressure belts (30o-35o) toward sub-polar low-pressure belts (60 o-65o) in both the hemisphere. Since there is more landmass in Northern Hemisphere compared to Southern Hemisphere the westerlies in the former case are more complex, and they are less influential in summers as compared to winter.
Wellington (New Zealand) is the only capital in the world that lies in the path of Roaring Forties.

Land and Sea Breezes only cover 20 to 30 km of the area including the coastal area. During daytime the land heats up faster than the nearby sea as a result low pressure is created over land and thus cool and moist winds blow from sea to land. This wind is called a sea breeze . There is a complete reversal in the direction of the wind during the night. As a result, winds blow from land to sea. This wind is called Land breeze. • Mountain and घाटी [Valley] Breeze - During daytime the air heats up and rises along the slope of the mountain. This is known as Valley Breeze (Anabatic flow). During the night the air gets cooler and heavier as a result it starts descending along the slope of the mountain. This is known as Mountain Breeze (Katabatic flow). सिरोको पवन [Sirocco: Blood rain wind] is a local wind that blows from the Sahara मरुस्थल [Desert] towards the Mediterranean Sea. The wind is dry, warm and sandy in nature. The equatorial region remains hot throughout the year and as a result, there is a lot of rainfall throughout the year. Hence, the equatorial region is covered with evergreen forests. These forests are found in abundance in three diverse regions of the world – (1) Amazon Basin – The region includes Brazil, Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, Colombia, Venezuela, Guyana and Suriname. (2) Congo Basin – The region includes the Republic of Congo, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and Democratic Republic of Congo. (3) Borneo- Mekong - Southeast Asia Basin - The region is composed of two sub-regions, the द्वीप [Island] of Borneo and the Mekong River.

Maximum plant species are found in the evergreen rainforests. Hardwood trees like – Rosewood, Aabnoos, Mahogany etc. are found in these forests. • Tropical पर्णपाती वन [Deciduous Forest] – They are also known as monsoonal forests. They are mostly found in India, northern Australia, Indonesia the Central America. There are two distinctive seasons (moist and dry) in these forests. India and its nearby regions experience three distinctive seasons thus even the forests of the area experience seasonal changes. The main flora of these forests includes Sal, Teak, Neem and Rosewood. Apart from these other trees, herbs and shrubs are also found. • Temperate Evergreen Forests – They are found in the coastal areas of mid-latitudes. They are normally found on the eastern sides of the continent such as south east USA, South China and southeastern Brazil. Temperate evergreen forests are dominated by specific species of trees. The trees have broad leaves and hardwood for example – Oak, Laurel, Magnolia, and Eucalyptus etc. • Mediterranean Forest – These forests are found in the mid-latitudes on the western and southwestern parts of the continent. They are located in regions receiving winter rainfall. Mediterranean forests are mostly found in the regions of Africa, Europe and Asia that lie in proximity to the Mediterranean Sea. These forests are also found in California and southwestern Australia. The main trees of the region are Cork, Oak, Olives, Plums, Chestnut, Pine etc. The Mediterranean region is famous for the production of Citrus fruits such as Grapes, Lemons, Oranges, Olives, Pears, Pomegranate, etc. •Temperate Coniferous Forests – Also known as टैगा वन [Taiga / Boreal Forest] Forest. They are found between 50 o to 60o North latitude. To their north they have tundra and to their south, they have deciduous forests. They are found in regions of North America, Eurasia and sub-polar regions. They are found in Canada, Europe, Asia and the USA. Temperate coniferous forests cover the largest area in the world. Important flora of the region includes – Deodar, Fir, Hemlock, Spruce, etc. In India, these forests are found in high Himalayan regions. •According to data from the World Food and Agriculture Statistical Yearbook, 2025 (Data - 2023). (3) Capillary Action – It is responsible for upward movement of water from wet areas to dry areas of the soil. The smaller the pore the higher the capillary action and vice versa.

If there is equitable distribution of the given subject then isopleths become very useful. Moreover, the use of isopleths becomes difficult if the subject is in constant fluctuation for exp. population density.
